paragraphs: A classifier can be built by combining several classifiers with nonnegative weights that sum to one. This paper studies how to bound the expected loss of such a combination. The question is how to connect what can be calculated from training data with the loss the combined classifier incurs beyond those observations.

The authors provide a PAC-Bayesian upper bound that applies to a broad family of loss functions. That family includes exponential loss and logistic loss, so the result is not restricted to counting incorrect predictions. Its significance is the ability to analyze classifier combinations under several ways of assigning a cost to their predictions.

The paper also reports numerical experiments with AdaBoost. In those experiments, the upper bound calculated from training data behaves similarly to the true loss estimated using test data. This is empirical evidence that the bound can reflect changes in predictive loss, alongside its theoretical role as an upper bound; it does not establish exact equality between the two.
neurips-2006-a-pac-bayes-risk-bound-for-.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian bound covers several losses for classifier combinations and empirically tracks test loss in AdaBoost experiments.

paragraphs: Maximum Margin Planning learns from demonstrations by constructing a cost function for a planning problem. A planner then chooses a policy that minimizes that cost. Training seeks costs under which the teacher’s demonstrated behavior is preferable to competing behavior, with a separation that depends on how much the alternatives differ from the desired result.

The original approach learns a linear mapping from supplied features to costs. This paper introduces MMPBOOST, which expands that representation by adding features through boosting. It uses the functional gradient descent interpretation of boosting to guide these additions, allowing simple binary classification or regression procedures to improve the imitation learning system.

This matters because learning a useful planning cost depends on the features available to express it. The contribution provides a way to improve those features within the learning process. The authors also extend the approach to structured maximum margin prediction and apply it to outdoor robot navigation and planning, as well as robotic legged locomotion.
neurips-2006-boosting-structured-predict.tldr: MMPBOOST adds learned features through boosting to improve cost learning from demonstrations for planning and structured prediction.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often requires approximating a distribution that is difficult to handle directly. The paper identifies a tradeoff between two existing approaches: methods based on sum-product message passing cover a relatively restricted collection of models, while mean field approximations apply more broadly but can produce poor solutions. The goal is to improve the latter approach.

The authors introduce a family of variational approximations specified through conditional distributions and based on mean field theory. These approximations are not usable by themselves. Their proposed role is within a combination with sequential Monte Carlo, and it is this combined construction that provides guaranteed improvements over conventional mean field.

Experiments examine inference of stable configurations in an Ising spin glass. On this problem, the resulting solutions can be substantially better than those from sum-product methods. The paper therefore offers both a guarantee relative to conventional mean field and empirical evidence against another class of inference methods, with the latter comparison demonstrated on the stated problem.
neurips-2006-conditional-mean-field-7024.tldr: Conditional mean field approximations combined with sequential Monte Carlo guarantee improvements over conventional mean field.

paragraphs: Kernel methods transform the representation of data so that classification can work well using linear decision functions in feature space. This paper asks how much of that space actually carries information relevant to the classification task. Its central result concerns whether a much smaller collection of directions can retain the useful information.

The authors show that a finite set of leading kernel principal components contains the relevant classification information up to negligible error, provided the kernel matches the underlying learning problem. That condition is central: the result describes what a suitably matched kernel can achieve. Such a kernel can both support good generalization and use feature space dimensions economically.

The paper also proposes an algorithm for recovering the relevant subspace and its dimensionality. This gives the theoretical result a practical role: examining the geometry created by a dataset and kernel, supporting model selection, and removing noise in feature space. These applications connect dimension reduction to the classification objective rather than treating compactness as an end in itself.
neurips-2006-denoising-and-dimension-red.tldr: When a kernel matches the task, a finite set of leading kernel PCA components can preserve nearly all relevant classification information.

paragraphs: A sensor network or team of robots must combine observations while the system it monitors keeps changing. This paper presents a distributed algorithm for approximate probabilistic inference in that setting. Network nodes jointly maintain a manageable representation of their belief about the system’s state, using a method called assumed density filtering.

At each time step, the nodes coordinate to incorporate observations collected across the network and then advance the estimate to the next time step. Communication failures create an additional difficulty: lost messages or disconnected parts of the network can leave different nodes with inconsistent beliefs about the same current state.

The authors develop distributed procedures that guarantee recovery of an informative, consistent distribution once communication resumes. The guarantee concerns reconciliation after communication is restored, which directly addresses the identified failure mode. Experiments use real sensor data from two deployments, one containing 25 cameras and the other 54 temperature sensors, grounding the approach in two different network sensing settings.
neurips-2006-distributed-inference-in-dy.tldr: A distributed inference method tracks changing systems and guarantees consistent, informative beliefs after interrupted communication resumes.

paragraphs: Earlier quadratic models of natural images produced model cells that responded strongly to edges and bars. This paper investigates whether learning from natural image patches can also yield features that represent more explicitly two-dimensional patterns, such as corners. The authors apply quadratic Independent Component Analysis to those patches.

They find that, apart from a small approximation error, the learned components compute conjunctions of two linear features. In plain language, a component represents a combination of two simpler visual features. These combinations appear to capture edges and bars as well as corner-like stimuli. For many components, the simpler features have receptive field characteristics resembling those of V1 simple cells.

The result links the structure learned from natural images to properties associated with visual processing. In particular, it suggests that unsupervised sparse coding could partly explain the development of V2 cells that prefer angles and corners. The claim is a possible partial explanation, supported by the learned feature structure, rather than a complete account of those cells.
neurips-2006-emergence-of-conjunctive-vi.tldr: Quadratic ICA learns combinations of visual features that may partly explain how angle- and corner-sensitive V2 cells develop.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data alongside a smaller set of labeled examples. Its effectiveness depends substantially on the graph that represents relationships among data points. This paper addresses how to learn the graph’s hyperparameters, making the choice of those relationships part of the learning procedure.

The proposed method targets harmonic energy minimization. It adjusts graph settings to minimize leave-one-out prediction error on labeled points: each labeled point serves as a prediction check when its own label is withheld. This supplies a criterion for choosing the graph using the labeled evidence that is already available.

The authors use gradient-based optimization and make gradient calculation more efficient through the matrix inversion lemma and carefully chosen precomputations. This computational contribution matters because graph learning requires evaluating how parameter changes affect prediction error. Experiments show that the learned graphs improve classification performance, supporting the value of tuning the graph rather than treating its construction as a fixed preliminary choice.
neurips-2006-hyperparameter-learning-for.tldr: Learning graph hyperparameters from leave-one-out label prediction improves a graph-based semi-supervised classifier in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to estimate parameters for continuous density hidden Markov models used in speech recognition. The learning objective follows the margin maximization idea associated with support vector machines. Its aim is to train the speech model through separation between alternatives, while retaining a representation suited to real-valued acoustic observations.

The approach specifically accommodates Gaussian mixture models for observations such as acoustic feature vectors. Its training objective is defined over positive semidefinite matrices and leads to a convex optimization problem. The authors emphasize that this formulation avoids spurious local minima, distinguishing it from the cited discriminative speech training frameworks.

Simple gradient-based methods can optimize the objective efficiently and scale to large problems. The reported phonetic recognition results on the TIMIT corpus are competitive. Taken together, the contributions connect a margin-based learning goal with an observation model appropriate for speech and an optimization formulation with favorable mathematical structure; the empirical claim is competitive performance, rather than a stated across-the-board improvement.
neurips-2006-large-margin-hidden-markov-.tldr: Large-margin training for continuous density HMMs yields a convex optimization problem and competitive phonetic recognition results.

paragraphs: Sequence prediction can require identifying whole segments, with properties that belong to a stretch of the sequence rather than a single position. This paper introduces Hidden Semi-Markov Support Vector Machines by extending Hidden Markov SVMs to semi-Markov chains. The extension allows predictions to use features describing complete segments.

Segment length is one example of information that the model can incorporate directly. This makes the representation useful for segmentation problems where the extent of a region matters. The paper also addresses the computational challenge through a technique that partitions the learning problem into subproblems, solves them independently, and efficiently recombines their partial solutions.

That decomposition enables learning from several thousand labeled sequences. The authors test the algorithm on gene structure prediction using a well-known model organism, and report results illustrating its potential for computational biology. The contribution therefore combines richer sequence modeling with a way to handle larger training collections, connecting the ability to describe segments with the ability to learn those descriptions at scale.
neurips-2006-large-scale-hidden-semi-mar.tldr: Hidden Semi-Markov SVMs use segment-level features and decomposed training to learn sequence segmentations from thousands of labeled sequences.

paragraphs: Two classifiers can be considered close when they rarely disagree on examples drawn from a particular distribution. This paper uses that probability of disagreement as a distance between classifiers. It then relates the number of examples needed for PAC learning to the doubling dimension of the resulting metric space.

This viewpoint brings the distribution of examples into the geometry used to analyze learning. The derived bounds imply known sample complexity results for halfspaces under a uniform distribution that are optimal up to a constant factor. The authors also prove a bound for any learning algorithm that returns a zero-error classifier whenever such a classifier is available.

That latter bound depends on the larger of the doubling dimension and the classifier family’s VC dimension, and strengthens the previous bound expressed using VC dimension alone. However, the two dimensions are not interchangeable: the paper shows that VC dimension cannot by itself bound doubling dimension. The results therefore establish both the usefulness and the distinct role of this geometric measure.
neurips-2006-learnability-and-the-doubli.tldr: The geometry of classifier disagreement yields PAC sample complexity bounds through doubling dimension, which VC dimension alone cannot bound.

paragraphs: Locally linear embedding constructs a lower-dimensional representation using local reconstruction relationships among neighboring data points. This paper modifies that approach by introducing multiple linearly independent weight vectors for each neighborhood. The change allows the embedding procedure to use several independent local reconstruction relationships within the same neighborhood.

The authors analyze the reconstruction weights and establish that the required independent vectors exist at each neighborhood. Their modified method, MLLE, is reported to be more stable. The paper also states a recovery property: MLLE can retrieve the ideal embedding when applied to points sampled from an isometric manifold, tying that result to a specific geometric condition on the data.

The method is compared with local tangent space alignment, and numerical examples demonstrate improvement and efficiency. The contribution combines a change to the information retained locally with analysis of when an ideal global representation can be recovered. The isometric-manifold condition belongs to that recovery statement; it should not be read as a claim that arbitrary datasets admit ideal recovery.
neurips-2006-mlle-modified-locally-linea.tldr: MLLE improves embedding stability using multiple local weight vectors and can recover an ideal embedding under an isometric-manifold condition.

paragraphs: A document can resemble another because they discuss the same broad subject, because they share particular words, or both. Topic models capture general subject matter by reducing a document to a smaller latent representation. This paper argues for retaining document-specific vocabulary alongside that abstraction when representing documents for retrieval.

The proposed probabilistic model separates a document into three components. One distribution accounts for common background words, a mixture of topics represents general content, and another distribution captures words treated as specific to that document. This gives shared vocabulary, broad themes, and document-specific wording distinct places in the same model.

The authors illustrate retrieval that matches documents at both the topic level and the specific-word level. They report an advantage over methods that use only general representations, such as topic models and latent-semantic indexing, or only word-level matching, such as TF-IDF. The stated benefit comes from combining these two kinds of evidence so that broad semantic similarity and particular wording can both contribute to a match.
neurips-2006-modeling-general-and-specif.tldr: A three-part document model combines background words, general topics, and document-specific vocabulary to improve retrieval matching.

paragraphs: Understanding transcriptional dynamics requires quantities that differ greatly in how easily they can be measured. Messenger RNA abundance and decay rates are relatively accessible, while active transcription factor concentrations and the sensitivity of target genes to those concentrations are difficult to observe. This paper seeks to infer those harder-to-measure quantities from gene expression.

The method starts with expression levels for a set of known targets of a given transcription factor. It represents the protein concentration as an unobserved function with a Gaussian process prior. Gene sensitivities, mRNA decay rates, and baseline expression levels enter the model as hyperparameters, connecting the hidden concentration to the available expression observations.

The authors apply the procedure to a human leukemia dataset, focusing on p53, and obtain results that agree well with biological studies. The contribution is a model-based route from observed target-gene expression to otherwise difficult biological quantities. Its setup relies on having a known set of target genes, which supplies the relationship needed for this inference.
neurips-2006-modelling-transcriptional-r.tldr: A Gaussian process model infers transcription factor activity and gene sensitivities from expression measurements of known target genes.

paragraphs: Online convex programming provides a common framework for sequential learning and decision problems, including classification, path selection, and game strategies. Existing no-regret algorithms address this general setting, but the paper identifies a shortage of flexible design tools compared with the more specialized problem of learning from expert advice.

For expert advice, convex potential functions provide a way to construct algorithms with different useful guarantees. The authors extend this design principle to online convex programming through a family called Lagrangian Hedging. These algorithms are based on a general class of potential functions and directly generalize familiar rules such as weighted majority and external-regret matching.

The paper proves regret bounds and demonstrates the algorithms learning one-card poker. Its central contribution is a recipe for generating a broader family of online learning rules, creating room to adapt algorithm design to properties of a problem or its data. The poker demonstration provides an application of that recipe alongside the theoretical guarantees.
neurips-2006-no-regret-algorithms-for-on.tldr: Lagrangian Hedging uses general potential functions to construct flexible no-regret algorithms for online convex programming.

paragraphs: Neural motor prostheses need to convert motor cortical activity into control of an artificial system. Much earlier decoding work focused on recovering hand motion directly, but a cursor or robot can have different physical dynamics. This paper explores decoding parameters of a physical model that generates movement.

The model represents two-dimensional hand motion as a point mass attached to idealized springs. Neural firing rates determine the nonlinear spring coefficients, so decoded activity controls the system’s physical parameters. The authors evaluate linear and nonlinear decoding algorithms using recordings from two monkeys performing two different tasks.

The decoded spring parameters produce accurate hand trajectories in comparison with state-of-the-art direct decoding methods. The generated movements also have frequency spectra closer to those of natural hand movement. That is the specific sense in which the paper calls the output more natural. The findings support incorporating physical dynamics into decoding, with the reported evidence coming from the stated monkey recordings and hand-motion model.
neurips-2006-nonlinear-physically-based-.tldr: Decoding neural activity into spring-model parameters produces accurate hand trajectories with frequency spectra closer to natural movement.

paragraphs: Learning systems often describe relationships between examples through a kernel computed from their input attributes. However, known relationships among examples can reveal additional correlations between the quantities being predicted. This paper develops Gaussian process models that use both sources of information within a single learning framework.

The approach combines reciprocal relational information with the attributes of individual instances. It does so through a covariance function that depends on the data, giving relational evidence a role in how the model represents correlations. The resulting formulation is a nonparametric Bayesian framework for supervised learning, with covariance as the point where the two information sources meet.

The authors also apply the framework to semi-supervised learning and report experiments on several real-world datasets that support its usefulness. The contribution broadens the information available to Gaussian process learning: predictions can reflect relationships supplied alongside the examples, as well as similarity inferred from their attributes. The empirical finding supports that combined approach in the tested settings.
neurips-2006-relational-learning-with-ga.tldr: A Gaussian process framework combines instance attributes and relational information through a data-dependent covariance function.

paragraphs: Simulation-based policy search chooses a policy from a given class by comparing how well candidates perform in simulated runs of a Markov decision process. For this selection to be reliable, empirical performance must reflect true policy value across the class being searched. This paper studies conditions that ensure that agreement.

The authors establish uniform convergence when the computation required to evaluate policies, transition dynamics, and rewards is bounded in the specified way. This supplies a route to guarantees based on computational restrictions. Earlier results instead used assumptions involving bounded pseudodimension and Lipschitz continuity, so the paper offers a different sufficient set of conditions.

The paper also examines why stronger restrictions are needed. Using minimax inequalities, it shows that bounded pseudodimension or fat-shattering dimension alone does not suffice. The positive and negative results work together: they identify conditions under which simulation estimates converge uniformly and demonstrate why familiar measures of class complexity, taken alone, cannot guarantee successful simulation-based policy search.
neurips-2006-sample-complexity-of-policy.tldr: Computational bounds ensure uniform convergence in simulation-based policy search, while certain complexity measures alone are insufficient.

paragraphs: A skill rating system must infer player ability from game outcomes. TrueSkill extends the Elo approach using a Bayesian model that tracks uncertainty about each player’s skill. This makes uncertainty part of the representation, alongside the estimate of ability itself, as the system interprets results.

The model explicitly accommodates draws, supports any number of competing entities, and can infer individual skills from team outcomes. Those capabilities let the same framework address several forms of competition. The authors express the model as a factor graph and use approximate message passing to perform inference about skills from the observed results.

Experiments provide evidence of better accuracy and faster convergence than Elo. The paper also reports experience operating TrueSkill within a large commercial online gaming service. Its contribution therefore includes both a broader probabilistic model of competition and evidence from evaluation and deployment. The comparative accuracy and convergence claims are experimental findings, while support for draws, multiple competitors, and team results describes the system’s modeling capabilities.
neurips-2006-trueskilltm-a-bayesian-skil.tldr: TrueSkill models skill uncertainty, draws, multiple competitors, and team results, with experimental improvements over Elo.

paragraphs: High-dimensional measurements can arise from a process described by relatively few variables. This paper seeks to recover the relationship between those measurements and the underlying process without paired input-output examples. The authors derive a cost functional for this unsupervised regression problem, with applications to identifying nonlinear systems.

They restrict the search to invertible observation functions. Under that restriction, the formulation has a compact representation and no suboptimal local minima. Approximation algorithms optimize the objective quickly and provide diagnostic bounds on solution quality. The method can also be interpreted as manifold learning that incorporates a prior on the low-dimensional coordinates.

This prior provides information about the underlying coordinates while the method searches for inverse observation functions linking measurements back to the process. Experiments demonstrate benefits in learning to track moving targets from raw sensor-network measurements and in an RFID tracking setting. The results support using coordinate priors and inverse-function estimation together, with the stated optimization advantages tied to the invertibility restriction.
neurips-2006-unsupervised-regression-wit.tldr: Unsupervised regression uses invertible observation functions and coordinate priors to recover low-dimensional processes from raw measurements.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable labeling in a general discrete random field is computationally hard. Convex relaxations make the problem more approachable by replacing it with a related optimization problem. This paper compares three existing formulations based on linear programming, quadratic programming, and second order cone programming.

The authors show that the particular quadratic and second order cone relaxations under study are equivalent. They also prove that the linear programming relaxation strictly dominates both in approximation quality. Thus, the greater flexibility of the other optimization forms does not, by itself, make these particular formulations stronger.

The analysis extends to a large family of second order cone relaxations and equivalent quadratic relaxations, all dominated by the examined linear program. Building on these findings, the authors propose new second order cone relaxations that strictly dominate the previous approaches. The contribution is both a comparison of existing approximation strength and a basis for designing stronger relaxations; it does not claim that the optimization category alone determines quality.
neurips-2007-an-analysis-of-convex-relax.tldr: An analysis ranks existing MAP relaxations by approximation strength and motivates stronger second order cone formulations.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a sparse linear model can still be learned after data undergo random linear compression. The motivation includes reducing how much information about the original data is revealed. The authors establish conditions under which regression on the compressed representation can recover the underlying sparse model.

For regression with an l1 penalty, they characterize how many random projections are needed to identify the true model’s nonzero coefficients with probability approaching one. They call this property sparsistence. They also establish persistence: asymptotically, the compressed regression procedure predicts as well as an oracle linear model. These are distinct claims about identifying relevant coefficients and achieving predictive performance.

The privacy analysis uses information-theoretic quantities to bound the rate of information communicated between compressed and original data. Those upper bounds decay to zero. The paper therefore connects model recovery, prediction, and information disclosure within one compression procedure. Its recovery claims depend on stated conditions, and the prediction and vanishing-information results are asymptotic rather than guarantees of perfect finite-sample recovery or secrecy.
neurips-2007-compressed-regression-2e040.tldr: Under established conditions, randomly compressed data support sparse regression recovery and asymptotic prediction guarantees with vanishing information-rate bounds.

paragraphs: Approximate inference methods differ in whether their answers are certified bounds or simply estimates. Mean field methods provide lower bounds, while certain convex relaxations provide upper bounds. Loopy belief propagation often gives accurate approximations, but generally does not guarantee which side of the true quantity its result lies on.

This paper proves a stronger statement for a class of attractive binary graphical models. For these models, the value associated with any fixed point of loopy belief propagation is a lower bound on the true likelihood. The scope is tied to that model class and to a fixed point; the statement does not turn arbitrary belief propagation outputs into bounds.

The authors establish the result using a loop series expansion and show how that expansion follows from a tree reparameterization description of belief propagation fixed points. Empirically, the bound is much better than naive mean field and requires no additional work beyond running belief propagation. The contribution gives an existing approximation a certified interpretation within the stated setting.
neurips-2007-loop-series-and-bethe-varia.tldr: For a class of attractive binary models, every loopy belief propagation fixed point provides a lower bound on the true likelihood.

paragraphs: Predicting missing entries in a partially observed matrix requires a model of the matrix’s observed and unobserved values. This paper assumes that the entire matrix is one sample from a matrix-variate t distribution. It introduces a predictive model built around that joint assumption, called a matrix-variate t model.

The authors show that the model generalizes a range of existing probabilistic models and automatically performs model selection that encourages sparse predictive models. Computation presents a challenge because the prior is non-conjugate, making prediction through the posterior mean or mode difficult. The proposed solution is an optimization procedure that successively minimizes a convex upper bound of the log-likelihood.

The authors describe this procedure as efficient and scalable, and report good predictive accuracy on toy data and the EachMovie dataset. The contribution joins a matrix-level probabilistic assumption with a practical optimization method. Its findings support the proposed model for missing-entry prediction in those experiments, while the whole-matrix distributional assumption defines how the prediction problem is represented.
neurips-2007-predictive-matrix-variate-t.tldr: A matrix-variate t model predicts missing entries, encourages sparse predictive models, and uses efficient sequential bound optimization.

paragraphs: Kernel machines can represent useful nonlinear relationships, but training them at large scale motivates more efficient representations. This paper proposes mapping inputs into a randomized, low-dimensional feature space and then training with existing fast linear methods. The transformation is designed to preserve the similarities expressed by a chosen kernel.

Specifically, inner products between transformed examples approximate the inner products associated with a user-specified shift-invariant kernel. This makes the random features a bridge between the desired kernel representation and linear learning algorithms. The authors explore two feature constructions and provide convergence bounds describing their ability to approximate various radial basis kernels.

On large-scale classification and regression tasks, linear algorithms using these features outperform the state-of-the-art large-scale kernel machines considered in the paper. The contribution combines approximation analysis with empirical evidence for a practical training strategy. Its central tradeoff is explicit: the features approximate the selected kernel’s similarities while allowing learning to proceed in a compact representation suited to fast linear methods.
neurips-2007-random-features-for-large-s.tldr: Random low-dimensional features approximate shift-invariant kernels so fast linear methods can tackle large-scale kernel learning tasks.

paragraphs: Simulated annealing is used to approach global optimization problems. This paper addresses guarantees for problems whose variables range continuously, rather than taking values from a finite set. The distinction matters because the performance results described as previously available concern discrete combinatorial optimization.

The authors introduce a general formulation of simulated annealing that permits finite-time performance guarantees for continuous variables. Their results apply universally to optimization problems on bounded domains. The bounded-domain condition is therefore part of the stated scope, while the finite-time focus concerns what can be guaranteed after a finite run rather than only in an eventual limit.

The analysis connects simulated annealing with convergence theory for Markov chain Monte Carlo on continuous domains. It is also motivated by statistical learning theory’s treatment of learning with specified accuracy and confidence in finite time. The contribution is a theoretical framework for assessing continuous-domain annealing through those ideas, giving its performance a finite-time interpretation within the stated bounded-domain setting.
neurips-2007-simulated-annealing-rigorou.tldr: A general simulated annealing formulation provides finite-time optimization guarantees for continuous problems on bounded domains.
